opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that a base model has learned an enormous number of concepts, but they're stored in a form that's really alien to us. They're distributed across neurons, they're superimposed on top of each other, and if you just look at raw activations you mostly see noise. The model clearly "knows" things, but that knowledge isn't legible.

What an interpreter model does is act as a translator between that internal representation space and something a human can actually reason about. You train it to take the base model's activations and map them onto descriptions, features, or concepts that are meaningful to us. So instead of staring at a vector of thousands of numbers, you get something like: "right now the model is representing the idea of deception," or "it's tracking that the user is a medical professional," or "it's thinking about this as a legal question."

And the reason that's useful goes beyond just understanding. Once you can name a concept and locate it reliably, you can start working with it. You can monitor it: is this concept firing when it shouldn't? You can debug with it: why did the model give this weird answer, and what was it actually attending to internally? And increasingly you can steer with it: turn a concept up or down, and see how the behavior changes.

I think the key insight is that you don't want humans hand-labeling millions of features. That doesn't scale. So you use a model to do the interpretation, because models are good at exactly this kind of pattern-to-language mapping. The interpreter makes the base model's concepts addressable. It gives you handles on them, and once you have handles, you can actually build tools, run audits, and fix problems in a way that's grounded in what the model is really doing rather than just what it outputs.

r001.rationale: The response says the interpreter maps base-model activations to human-meaningful descriptions, features, or concepts, and makes the base model’s concepts addressable.

fable-5.1.text:
The way I think about it is that a base model already has these concepts inside it. The problem is they're sitting there as directions in activation space, with no labels and no handles. If you crack the model open and look at the raw activations, you see millions of numbers, and nothing in there tells you "this one is the concept of a legal contract" or "this one is the model noticing the user is frustrated."

An interpreter model is a second model whose whole job is to be the translator. You feed it the internal state of the base model, and it produces a human-readable description of what's going on. So instead of asking a researcher to stare at feature activations and guess, you can just ask the interpreter, "What is this feature? When does it fire? Give me examples." It turns something you'd need a week of manual probing to understand into something you can query in a few seconds.

What makes that useful, rather than just interesting, is that the labels become handles. Once you have a name for a concept and a reliable way to find it, you can do things with it. You can monitor it, so if a feature corresponding to deception or to some unsafe behavior lights up during a conversation, you see that happen in real time. You can steer on it, dialing a concept up or down and watching how the output changes. You can audit it, checking whether the thing the model says it's doing matches the internal state.

The other piece people underestimate is scale. A frontier model has way too many internal features for humans to label by hand. So the interpreter has to be automated, and it has to be good enough that you trust its explanations. We spend a lot of effort on that second part, scoring whether the interpreter's description actually predicts when the feature fires on new data. If the explanation doesn't predict behavior, it's a story, not an interpretation.

So in short: the base model holds the concepts, the interpreter gives them names and gives you a way to verify those names are right, and that's what turns a pile of activations into something an engineer can actually work with.

r001.rationale: The response says the interpreter translates the base model’s internal state into human-readable descriptions, but it does not state that concepts in the interpreter model map to corresponding concepts in the base model.

astra-6.text:
I think of the interpreter as a bridge between the representations inside a base model and the concepts we can actually reason about. The base model has learned a lot of structure, but that structure isn’t necessarily organized into neat, human-readable labels. A concept might be spread across many activations, and a single activation might participate in several concepts.

An interpreter model tries to translate that internal structure into something useful: what seems to be represented here, when does it show up, and how does it relate to the model’s behavior? Then you can start asking more targeted questions—whether the model is tracking a particular distinction, for example, or whether a representation changes across contexts.

The important thing is that a plausible description isn’t enough. You want to test whether the interpretation predicts what happens on new examples, and ideally whether intervening on that representation changes behavior in the way you’d expect. That’s what turns an interesting label into a tool you can work with.

r001.rationale: The response describes the interpreter as translating the base model’s internal structure into useful descriptions, but does not clearly state that concepts in the interpreter model map to corresponding concepts in the base model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of the interpreter as a bridge between the representations inside a base model and concepts that a person can actually reason about. The base model may encode something useful, but it doesn’t necessarily encode it in a form that comes with a clean label or explanation. An interpreter tries to make that structure legible: what does this representation respond to, when does it show up, and how does it relate to other concepts?

The important step is making those interpretations testable. If we think we’ve identified a concept, can we predict where it will activate? And if we intervene on it, does the model’s behavior change in the way we expect? That’s what turns a plausible description into something useful for understanding and potentially steering the model.
